items.title: Campaigners call for emergency government support as average annual energy bill in Britain set to hit £2,166 – business live
items.summary:
Regulator Ofgem announces that the typical annual gas and electricity bill will rise by 26% in January – described as ‘deeply worrying’ by campaigners

As well as short-term support measures for households this winter, experts are calling for a more decisive shift towards renewable energy sources, to reduce Britain’s reliance on gas.

Charles McAllister, director of the Green Gas Taskforce, said:

Today’s price cap rise shows how exposed households remain to imported energy - the answer is to generate more at home.

Biomethane, made from farms and food waste, is already flowing through our grid - enough to heat around a million homes - but NESO [National Energy System Operator] has just cut its outlook for biomethane because of policy uncertainty.

The implications of the staggering 26% incoming energy price hike will be sinking in for many older households in financial hardship already under considerable strain. With the typical annual energy bill for a home rising to £2,166 from January, urgent emergency support is needed to help everyone, including people past State Pension age living on low incomes meet surging costs this winter.

Continue reading...
items.t: Rise in energy bills in Britain to £2,166 is ‘an impossible high’ for millions of households; stocks tumble as AI rally fizzles – business live

items.title: Walmart’s shopper base is shifting: High earners lead its gains as low-income shoppers turn to Amazon
items.summary:
Walmart is known for its bargains, but its growth increasingly comes from shoppers who don’t strictly need them. Six-figure households like a good deal, too.

Upper-income households led Walmart’s U.S. market-share gains, the company said Nov. 19 as it reported fiscal third-quarter results . Revenue rose 5.2% to $188.8 billion from $179.5 billion a year earlier and topped Wall Street’s forecasts for both sales and profit.

E-commerce did the heavy lifting. U.S. online sales rose 23%, the 11th straight quarter up more than 20%, while global e-commerce grew 17%.

“We delivered strong results, growing our core business and gaining market share,” CEO John Furner said in the release. Walmart raised its full-year outlook for the third time this year and now expects net sales growth of 4.9% to 5.2% and adjusted earnings per share of $2.84 to $2.89, up from $2.80 to $2.87.

Not everything accelerated. U.S. comparable sales rose 2.9%, well below the 4.5% gain a year earlier, and the new outlook came in more conservative than analysts expected, the Associated Press reported .

The split matters well beyond Bentonville. With more than 150 million customers shopping its stores or website each week, Walmart is one of the clearest windows into American spending heading into the holidays, and right now that window shows higher earners stepping up while others pull back.

Higher earners, younger members 

Furner said in February that most of Walmart’s share gains came from households earning more than $100,000 , and in June he told reporters that higher-income customers were visiting more…
items.t: Walmart’s shopper base is shifting: High earners lead its gains as low-income shoppers turn to Amazon

items.title: Europe has spent $15.9 billion trying to win the quantum race. Is it enough?
items.summary:
In September 2017, Google researcher Austin Fowler stood before a room of quantum engineers at a conference in College Park, Md., and admitted something rarely heard from Big Tech: He was stuck. Quantum computers make mistakes constantly, and every error must be caught within a millionth of a second before the whole calculation collapses. The best chip available was still 10 times too slow, Fowler said. Many in the room left convinced the problem might never be solved.

But across the Atlantic, on a quiet street in Cambridge, a five-person startup was developing its own solution to the problem. Steve Brierley, a Cambridge University research fellow, had founded Riverlane from his kitchen table the year before. “Even Google can’t solve this problem,” he recalls thinking when he heard Fowler’s admission. In 2024, Riverlane ran what it describes as the world’s first low-latency quantum error-correction experiment, decoding errors in under a microsecond— fast enough to keep the machine running.

Today, Riverlane employs nearly 200 people and works with more than 60% of the world’s quantum computer makers.

With U.S. tech companies dominating the digital economy, and China and America pulling ahead in the race for AI supremacy, quantum computing represents a rare opportunity for Europe to establish itself at the forefront of a transformative technology. The European Commission’s Quantum Europe Strategy, aims to make the continent a global quantum leader by 2030, and McKinsey estimates the technology could create $2.7 trillion of economic value worldwide by 2035.

The most…
items.t: Europe has spent $15.9 billion trying to win the quantum race. Is it enough?

items.title: After $26 billion in gifts, MacKenzie Scott is still worth $27 billion—and just gave Atlanta students $8 million more
items.summary:
Four years ago, MacKenzie Scott gave $8 million to Achieve Atlanta, a nonprofit that helps Atlanta public school students pay for and finish college. Last week, the organization announced she had done it again , with a second $8 million gift that brings her total support to $16 million.

It is one of two gifts Scott made to Georgia education nonprofits this month, together worth $12.5 million. The donor has given away more than $26 billion since her 2019 divorce from Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, yet is still worth more than $27 billion, largely because Amazon stock keeps rising.

For an Atlanta Public Schools graduate pursuing a bachelor’s degree, the need-based Achieve Atlanta scholarship can be worth up to $20,000 over four years . Students in two-year colleges and technical programs can receive $1,500 a year for up to four semesters.

The nonprofit also helps students choose colleges, work through the application process, and find their first jobs. Since 2015, it has awarded more than $75 million in scholarships.

An independent evaluation by researchers affiliated with Georgia State University’s Georgia Policy Labs found that 91% of Achieve Atlanta scholars returned for a second semester of college. Among peers who also graduated from Atlanta Public Schools, had similar academic and demographic backgrounds, and enrolled in college without the program’s support, 77% did.

The gap narrows over time but holds. Six years after high school, 42% of scholars had graduated, compared with 36% of similar peers.

“The repeated investment by Scott is a testament to the success of…
items.t: After $26 billion in gifts, MacKenzie Scott is still worth $27 billion—and just gave Atlanta students $8 million more

items.title: GTA VI’s $3.79 billion debut has Zuckerberg joking and Musk laughing, but Take-Two investors still want more
items.summary:
Mark Zuckerberg wanted to know which version of Grand Theft Auto VI he’d bought. On Nov. 20, the Meta CEO posted an edited screenshot on X of one of the game’s in-game prompts: a mission to “pick up groceries” with a pink heart and the line “Priscilla will appreciate this.” His caption: “Wait which version did I get?”

Elon Musk, the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, replied with a laughing emoji. The exchange capped the first full day of what is now the biggest entertainment launch on record.

Rockstar Games, the Take-Two Interactive label behind the franchise, said GTA VI generated $3.79 billion in worldwide retail sales on its Nov. 19 release day , based on company estimates. That is more than four times the roughly $800 million GTA V took in on its first day in 2013. The game also sold 32.5 million units before it went on sale.

For scale, the day-one retail figure is more than half of the $6.66 billion in net revenue Take-Two reported for its entire fiscal year ended March 2026 . Retail sales count what consumers spent, not what Take-Two keeps after platform holders and retailers take their cut. Still, the opening validates a bet CEO Strauss Zelnick described to Fortune only as “expensive” , and one former Take-Two CEO Ben Feder called the last pre-AI blockbuster of its kind .

Wall Street wants more than a record opening 

The sales kept coming after launch day. Research firm Alinea Analytics estimates the game sold through 44.9 million copies by the end of its opening weekend , grossing more than $4 billion. Take-Two has not confirmed those figures.

Investors were less…
items.t: GTA VI’s $3.79 billion debut has Zuckerberg joking and Musk laughing, but Take-Two investors still want more

items.title: Exclusive: Meta and Amazon discuss ending Muse shopping bot blockade, as ads, search emerge as key issues
items.summary:
Amazon and Meta Platforms are in ongoing discussions over a potential deal to connect Meta’s popular Muse AI agent to the e-commerce giant’s online store and end a blockade of the shopping bot imposed by Amazon two months ago.

The two tech giants have held talks on multiple occasions, and two major factors being negotiated are how the companies will handle search results and advertising in any deal, according to people familiar with the matter. Discussions are fluid, and it’s unclear if or how soon an agreement will be struck. There are numerous issues, ranging from Amazon’s own AI shopping ambitions to how exactly Muse would connect to Amazon. A major threat Muse poses to Amazon is that, in theory, it would bypass advertisements on Amazon’s website, which are a large source of revenue for the retailer.

Amazon is worried about losing advertising revenue and about the quality of the product search results Muse would surface, and executives are also concerned that shopping agents like Muse will weaken the relationship Amazon has with consumers, the people said. Any deal between Amazon and Meta is expected to require sign-off from the CEOs of both companies, they said.

Meta and Amazon declined to comment. The negotiations are being closely followed because they have major implications for the future of online shopping and represent an important test case for how large corporations respond to the advent of AI agents. As agents like Muse become more widely used, companies like Amazon are scrambling to understand how the bots alter typical shopping patterns as well as the…
items.t: Exclusive: Meta and Amazon discuss ending Muse shopping bot blockade, as ads, search emerge as key issues

items.title: Going home for Thanksgiving? For a record 25.2 million young adults, that just means walking downstairs
items.summary:
Thanksgiving is one of the most stressful and busiest times to travel. But for a record number of young adults, that trip looks less like a three-hour flight and more like a two-minute walk from their childhood bedrooms.

According to a report from Realtor.com released Monday , the regions Americans have long moved to for cheaper housing are now where young adults are most likely to be moving back in with their parents. 

The share of 18- to 34-year-olds living with their parents rose 1.4 percentage points in both the South and the Midwest in 2025, to 32.3% and 31.7%, which were the largest increases of any region. But in the Northeast, where living at home has long been most common, the share fell 2.3 points to 36.9%, its lowest level since 2010.

“This is not a coastal problem that has stayed coastal; it has spread to even the more-accessible parts of the country,” wrote Hannah Jones, the Realtor.com senior economist who wrote the report.

Realtor.com 

Nationally, a record 25.2 million young adults lived with their parents last year, about 1 in 3 , a figure Realtor.com first reported in June. 

It’s also not just young people moving into their parents’ home. Geoffrey Sanzenbacher, an economist at Boston College’s Center for Retirement Research , found that the share of 25- to 34-year-olds hosting their parents rose from 1.6% in 1996 to 4% in 2025.

About 22% of Americans lived in a multigenerational household in 2024, up from 13% in 1970. When the Pew Research Center asked adults in these households why they live together, financial issues were the most common answer,…
items.t: Going home for Thanksgiving? For a record 25.2 million young adults, that just means walking downstairs

items.title: Ukraine’s biggest steelmaker has battled years of Russian bombardment—now it faces a new threat
items.summary:
Wind the clock back 14 years and Ukraine was a country on a different path. The UEFA European Championship, cohosted with Poland, had provided a major international showcase for Ukraine and reinforced its ambitions to become more closely integrated with the European political and economic community. A European Union–Ukraine Association Agreement had been drafted, promising greater access to EU markets, visa-free movement, and greater alignment with EU standards. There was optimism that Ukraine could break with its post-Soviet political traditions and move more firmly into Europe’s economic and regulatory sphere

One of Ukraine’s most important industries remained a major force, despite concerns about stagnation and a lack of modernization. Steel production stood at 32.8 million tonnes (36 million tons) in 2013, and the country’s largest steel producer, and then largest private- sector employer, Metinvest, had appointed a new chief executive, Yuriy Ryzhenkov. Ryzhenkov is a man who has steelmaking DNA running through him.

“Why the steel industry?” he asks. “Very easy. My father, mother, uncle, aunt—they’re all steel engineers. My grandmother was a coal plant chemical engineer, which is also part of the steel industry. My grandfather was in the coal industry, but mainly coal for steel. So it was kind of inevitable. I tried to resist it by going into IT, but it didn’t work out in the end.”

A new CEO usually has a straightforward to-do list: a strategy reset, meetings with investors, and some thinking about which new products and markets to explore.

Preparing to navigate a…
items.t: Ukraine’s biggest steelmaker has battled years of Russian bombardment—now it faces a new threat

items.title: Best Buy’s new CEO inherits its fastest sales growth in five years and a 49% stock rally
items.summary:
Jason Bonfig’s first earnings report as Best Buy CEO came with numbers the retailer hasn’t posted in years. Comparable sales rose 6.1% in the fiscal third quarter, the strongest growth in five years, and the company raised its full-year outlook for the second straight quarter.

Investors had already started betting on a recovery. Best Buy shares are up nearly 49% this year as of Nov. 24, a sharp turn for a company whose sales had fallen in 14 of the 16 quarters before its CEO change was announced in April, according to Reuters.

Bonfig, who succeeded Corie Barry on Nov. 1, now has to prove the rebound can outlast a holiday season propped up by blockbuster game launches and pricier laptops.

Best Buy beat on revenue and earnings 

Revenue for the quarter ended Oct. 31 rose 5.8% to $10.24 billion, according to the company’s third-quarter earnings release . Adjusted earnings per share climbed 16% to $1.62.

Both figures topped Wall Street’s forecasts. CNBC reported that analysts surveyed by LSEG expected adjusted EPS of $1.49 on revenue of $9.90 billion.

Best Buy now expects fiscal 2027 revenue of $43 billion to $43.3 billion, up from $42.3 billion to $42.8 billion. It raised its comparable-sales forecast to 3.4% to 4%, from 1.9% to 3%, and its adjusted EPS outlook to $6.90 to $7.05, from $6.70 to $6.90.

Higher prices and game launches drove the quarter 

Computing and mobile phones did the heaviest lifting, along with newer categories such as AI glasses and trading cards. Much of the computing gain came from price rather than volume: Bonfig said on the earnings call that…
items.t: Best Buy’s new CEO inherits its fastest sales growth in five years and a 49% stock rally

items.title: What’s the most sustainable way to eat fish? Forget it. There isn’t one | George Monbiot

Don’t take the bait offered up by ‘conservation’ charities. Fishing is about as good for our ecosystems as tobacco is for our health

Drumroll please. I am about to unveil the species of fish that’s best to eat if you want to protect the living seas. Ta-dah! It’s … I hope that clears things up. Unfortunately, over the past few years, a noisy industry has developed to tell you otherwise. You’re doing the planet a favour if you eat mackerel, sorry, cod, I mean haddock, no coley, make that pollack – oh, whoops! These choices might make you feel better about yourself. But they do nothing but harm to marine wildlife. The fish you should choose is none of the above.

Cause, could I introduce you to effect? In April, the Marine Conservation Society, through its Good Fish Guide, suggested you stop eating cod and eat hake instead. Six months later, it lamented that hake is now overexploited thanks to “increased fishing pressure”, and…

items.title: Backed by Samsung, SK Hynix, and the Korean government, Rebellions CEO Sunghyun Park wants to prove sovereign AI pays off
items.summary:
Few corporate rivalries are as fierce as the one between Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. The world’s leading manufacturer of memory chips and the world’s leading manufacturer of high-bandwidth memory, respectively, are fighting for the title of South Korea’s most valuable company. In one area, though, the two are on the same team: Both back Rebellions, the $2.3 billion chip startup cofounded by Sunghyun Park—a veteran of Intel , SpaceX, and Morgan Stanley—that fronts South Korea’s push for sovereign silicon or AI chips that don’t depend on market leader Nvidia or any other U.S. or Chinese company.

Park’s company sits at the center of government policy. “AI requires huge capital and huge talent,” he says. “Instead of having multiple players compete, the Korean government said, ‘We need one champion. SK Hynix , please help him. Samsung, please help him. SK Telecom, KT’—top two data center companies—‘please become Rebellions’ customers.’”

Rebellions may be the clearest test of whether sovereign AI can produce something more than an expensive also-ran . Korea is funneling its best resources toward Rebellions: Samsung’s foundries, SK Hynix’s memory , and government money. The Korea National Growth Fund co-led Rebellions’ $400 million round in March.

Will it pay off? Rebellions eventually wants public investors to back a risky bet on a chip startup in a market that—for now—is skeptical of AI stocks. Still, Park is hopeful. Rebellions’ backers make it “more powerful compared to any other player in the United States,” he says. But market volatility and a wave of shelved data…
items.t: Backed by Samsung, SK Hynix, and the Korean government, Rebellions CEO Sunghyun Park wants to prove sovereign AI pays off

items.title: Council tax and stamp duty: both are a disaster zone. Scrap them and start from scratch | Polly Toynbee
items.summary:
These ancient and often grossly unfair taxes are stifling the economy and young people. It’s long past time for radical reform

When voters were asked in 2020 which tax they would cut first, council tax came out on top, and rightly so. Still, it’s taken six years for an array of Labour and Liberal Democrat MPs to call for reforms to this most grotesquely unjust tax.

Prompted by a public petition organised by the campaign Fairer Share, a Westminster Hall debate heard calls for a review into property taxes, which would lay out options for replacing council tax and stamp duty land tax. Labour MPs were among those who have signed a letter to Downing Street calling for property tax reform to be a priority in Andy Burnham’s upcoming 10-year plan. Among flotillas of economists and thinktanks who signed the letter is Lord O’Neill, a Burnham adviser and former Goldman Sachs economist, who calls UK property taxation “utterly nonsensical”. Burnham has frequently backed reform of the “highly regressive” council tax and stamp duty, labelling them as “a tax on the aspiration of young people”.

Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

items.t: Council tax and stamp duty: both are a disaster zone. Scrap them and start from scratch | Polly Toynbee

items.title: Children of the revolution: how the north of England is defining modern men’s fashion
items.summary:
Once the historic centre of the textile industry, the north is now home to a host of a provenance-driven labels. But is there a specific northern menswear look? And what does it all mean for the mad-fer-it stereotypes?

In 2026, clothing has proved more important to Andy Burnham’s political identity than that of any British prime minister since Margaret Thatcher. He is a loyal Clarks and Adidas wearer, whose Howick worker’s jacket hangs in Manchester’s People’s History Museum. His ousting of Keir Starmer – launched shortly before being photographed jogging in a replica Everton shirt – has been memorialised as the “casual coup”. In one telling, the reason for this is simple: he’s a man from the north.

That Burnham is the first born-and-bred northern male PM since Harold Wilson last swished his Gannex raincoat out of Downing Street goes some way to explaining his higher interest in clothing. It’s not necessarily that all men in the south care less about clothing, or that all men in the north do – but that many men from the north express it in such a distinctive, even unified, way.

Continue reading...
items.t: Children of the revolution: how the north of England is defining modern men’s fashion

items.title: How freaked out should we be? After mass outages, experts tell us how close we are to ‘doomsday’
items.summary:
As tech, travel and banking failures sweep the US, analysts and cyber-security directors discuss AI, underfunding and what keeps them up at night

Grounded flights. Bank websites crashing. Microsoft Outlook outages grinding business operations to a halt. Zoom, Ikea, and PokerStars websites hacked. In the past weeks, there’s been a distinct sense that the complex systems that undergird our daily life might be on the verge of total collapse. Or, at the very least, they seem pretty wobbly.

Even those who aren’t prone to conspiracy theories have been wondering out loud if these recent disruptions are somehow connected. Speculation runs wild about targeted cyber-attacks by Iranian hackers, or AI agents autonomously hacking critical (air traffic, banking) and not-so-critical (the Ikea website) infrastructure.

items.title: Why more Americans are choosing to pay over time
items.summary:
Paying with a credit card for lunch is routine today. It wasn’t always so. In a 1993 television report covering Burger King’s trial acceptance of credit cards, one customer objected, saying, “I think it’s pretty bad if you have to use a credit card when you go to a fast food restaurant. For something as little as $3.10.” Her objection assumed using credit for a small purchase meant you could not afford it. Newer payment tools face that same assumption today, even though the ways people manage everyday spending have changed. 

Today we see a major shift in how people across income levels access wages they have already earned and use deferred-payment options instead of traditional financing like credit cards. Block recently surveyed deferred-payment users, finding that 49% used cash advances or early wage access in the past year, alongside growing adoption of buy now, pay later. Survey findings also show about two in five Afterpay Pay in 4 and Pay Monthly users reported household incomes of $100,000 or more, underscoring that these tools reach across income brackets rather than serving only people without other options. 

The common thread behind both habits is timing. People often have money on the way that has not hit their account yet, and they use these tools to line up an expense with an incoming paycheck. By our estimate, U.S. workers at any given time have earned about $260 billion in wages they have not yet been paid. Among surveyed deferred-payment users, 65% financed an expense at least once in the past year because money was coming from a paycheck, refund, or…
items.t: Why more Americans are choosing to pay over time
